title: Lab 7 – Turner, Klinefelter, PCOS, hypogonadism
html:
Source: LP 7.pdf – 5 pages

Turner syndrome- clinical picture #1

  • Somatic anomalies
  • - lymphedema of the extremities (infancy)
  • - typical facies: micrognathia, a fish-like mouth with a narrow, high-arched palate,
  • hypertelorism, epicanthus, ptosis, strabismus, prominent, low-set ears
  • - short, thick, and webbed neck, low posterior hairline
  • - broad chest with widely spaced inverted nipples, scoliosis, multiple pigmented nevi
  • - cubitus valgus (Madelung deformity), short fourth metacarpals+ metatarsals
  • Short Stature- mean final height in 45,X0 patients is 143 cm ( 133–153 cm)
  • Gonadal Dysgenesis
  • - The gonads: ovarian follicles undergo premature apoptosis resulting in fibrous streaks
  • ->primary ovarian insufficiency
  • - The genital tract and external genitalia are female in character but immature.
  • - Puberty does not ensue spontaneously-> primary amenorrhea, sexual infantilism
  • Turner syndrome- complications
  • - Infertility
  • - Osteoporosis
  • - Increased risk of:
  •  celiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis, DM, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory
  • bowel disease
  •  recurrent otitis media
  •  cardiovascular defects—coarctation of aorta, nonstenotic bicuspid aortic valve, other
  • left-sided congenital heart defects
  •  kidney anomalies- horseshoe kidney, duplication of the renal pelvis and ureter, and
  • hydronephrosis secondary to uteropelvic obstruction.
  • Turner syndrome- investigations
  • - FSH, LH ↑ + ↓ E2
  • - ultrasonography of the pelvis or MRI: rudimentary ovaries/streak gonads, small uterus
  • - Barr test - negative
  • - karyotype analysis- the definitive procedure: 45,X0/mosaicism
  • - X-ray findings: shortening of the fourth metacarpal, scoliosis
  • - bone densitometry: osteoporosis
  • - echocardiography or MRI: to monitor aortic diameter and cardiovascular status
  • - intravenous urography or renal sonography: to detect a surgically correctable renal
  • abnormality.

Turner syndrome- management #2

  • - Although the short stature is not due to ↓ GH (it is related to haploinsufficiency of the
  • SHOX -short stature homeobox gene on the X chromosome), administration of high-dose
  • biosynthetic human GH results in an increase in final height-> give recombinant GH 45–
  • 50 μg/kg/day.
  • - In patients who have been treated with GH and have achieved an acceptable height,
  • estrogen replacement therapy should start between 11 and 12 years of age with low-
  • dose, increasing to adult dosing over 2–3 years (the transdermal route is preferred),
  • adding progesterone once breakthrough bleeding occurs, or after 2 years of estrogen
  • treatment.
  • - Treatment of complications.
  • Sex hormone replacement therapy- principles
  • A. Treatment of ovarian insufficiency with PREPUBERTAL onset- develop+ maintain
  • secondary sexual characteristics (breast development and feminization), induce growth
  • spurt, induce bone mass acquisition+ maintain bone mass.
  • - Estrogens can be administered as 17β-estradiol, estradiol valerate, conjugated estrogens, or
  • ethinyl estradiol- EE (the main estrogen used in combined oral contraceptive pills). E should
  • initially be administered alone; the dosage should be increased progressively, in order to
  • mimic natural puberty (e.g. start with EE 5 μg/day and increase to 10–20 μg/day). E can be
  • administered from day 1 to day 25. The optimal age to start replacement therapy= 12 years.
  • - 10 mg of medroxyprogesterone acetate/dydrogesterone are then added from day 12–14 to
  • day 25 after physical signs of estrogen effect are noted and breakthrough bleeding occurs (and
  • always within 6 months after initiating E); no treatment is given from day 25->the end of the
  • month. Withdrawal bleedings usually occur within a few days after stopping the treatment.
  • - Coexisting GH deficiency-> first treat de GH deficiency, then add estrogen therapy.
  • B. Treatment of ovarian insufficiency with POSTPUBERTAL onset: maintain secondary sex
  • characteristics (e.g., vulvar and vaginal lubrication), prevent osteoporosis, abolish
  • vasomotor symptoms and protects against cardiovascular risk.
  • -Estrogens and progestins can be administered in a sequential scheme or as a continuous
  • regimen. Examples of regimens:
  • CYCLO-PROGYNOVA® (21 tb): Estradiol valerate 2 mg (11 tb) and estradiol valerate 2 mg +
  • norgestrel 0.5 mg (10 tb)
  • FEMOSTON® 2/10 or 1/10 (28 tb): Estradiol (2 mg/1 mg) 14 tb + estradiol (2 mg/1 mg and
  • dydrogesterone) 14 tb
  • -Estrogens may be administered alone (in the absence of progesterone or progestins) only in
  • adolescents or women without a uterus .
  • -Clomiphene citrate/ Pulsatile GnRH infusion pumps/ recombinant FSH+ hCG treatment- if
  • fertility is desired (in secondary (central) ovarian insufficiency).

Contraindications to HRT #3

  • • Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding
  • • Pregnancy
  • • Active deep venous thrombosis
  • ABSOLUTE
  • • Active endometrial cancer
  • • Breast cancer
  • • Past history of endometrial cancer
  • • Family or past history of thromboembolism
  • • Ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease
  • RELATIVE
  • • Active liver disease
  • • Hypertriglyceridemia
  • Klinefelter syndrome- clinical picture
  • - Tall stature (↑ leg length); abnormal skeletal proportions that are not truly eunuchoid:
  • pubis-to-floor height is greater than crown-to-pubis height, but arm span is less than
  • total height (not secondary to androgen deficiency but is probably related to the
  • underlying chromosomal abnormality)
  • - Small (<2 cm in longest axis, and 4 mL in volume), firm testes-> primary hypogonadism
  • - Gynecomastia (50%)
  • ANDROGEN
  • - Reduced libido and erectile dysfunction, reduced facial hair
  • DEFICIENCY
  • - Infertility
  • - Penis and scrotum -varying degrees of development during puberty
  • - Osteoporosis
  • - Cognitive impairment, learning disabilities, poor impulse control, feeling of inadequacy,
  • and dissocial behavior are also common.
  • Klinefelter syndrome- investigations
  • - FSH, LH ↑, FSH>LH, T ↓
  • - Semen analysis: Azoospermia/ oligozoospermia
  • - Barr test: positive
  • - Karyotype analysis: 47,XXY in 80%; higher grade chromosomal aneuploidies (48,XXXY) or
  • 46,XY/47,XXY mosaicism in the remainder.
  • - Testicular ultrasound: ↓ volume of testis

Klinefelter syndrome- management #4

  • • It’s directed toward androgen replacement therapy.
  • • May need surgical reduction of gynecomastia.
  • • Fertility: intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), using testicular spermatozoa from men
  • with Klinefelter’s syndrome (sperm may be extracted directly from the testes in about half of
  • the patients), has resulted in successful pregnancies with a live birth rate of up to 20%.
  • • However, couples should be counselled about the ↑ risk of chromosomal abnormalities in
  • offspring.
  • Androgen replacement therapy- principles
  • Goals:
  • - Induction of puberty and then maintenance of secondary sexual characteristics.
  • - Improve libido and sexual function, mood and well-being, muscle mass and strength and
  • prevent osteoporosis in ♂ with testicular failure occurring after puberty.
  • Side Effects:
  • - Gynecomastia, erythrocytosis, sleep apnea, fluid retention may result in worsening
  • symptoms in those with underlying congestive cardiac failure or hepatic cirrhosis.
  • Absolute Contraindications: prostatic carcinoma, breast cancer
  • Relative Contraindications: benign prostate hyperplasia, polycythemia, sleep apnea
  • ! Baseline and 6-12 month interval measurements of PSA, FBC, ASAT, ALAT, GGT, ALP and lipid
  • profile should be done in patients treated with androgens.
  • Options:
  • - Testosterone enanthate or cyclopentyl propionate (cypionate)- 75–100 mg weekly IM.
  • - Testosterone undecanoate (Nebido®) 1000 mg, a long-acting form- IM every 3 months
  • - A testosterone gel (AndroGel 1%; Testim 1%) that is applied daily to the abdomen,
  • shoulders, or upper arms also results in physiologic concentrations of testosterone.
  • - In hypogonadal adolescents , androgen therapy is usually withheld until they reach 13
  • years of age (may cause premature fusion of the epiphyses in an adolescent, which may
  • result in some loss of potential height). Therapy may be initiated with 50 mg of
  • testosterone esters (enanthate/cypionate) IM every 4 weeks and gradually increased to
  • a maintenance dose of 75–100 mg every week or 150–200 mg every 2 weeks. In cases of
  • coexisting GH deficiency-> first treat de GH deficiency, then add androgen therapy
  • !!Androgen replacement therapy does not restore fertility, it suppresses normal
  • spermatogenesis-> men with secondary hypogonadism who desire fertility may be treated
  • with exogenous gonadotrophins (hCG, FSH)/ pulsatile GnRH infusion pumps to initiate and
  • maintain spermatogenesis.

Terminology #5

  • AMENORRHEA= absence of periods
  • a) primary- failure of menarche by the age of 16 years.
  • b) secondary- the cessation of menses for >6 months in women who had previously
  • menstruated OR no menses for > 3 cycles in an individual with previous regular menses.
  • OLIGOMENORRHEA= reduction in the frequency of menses to <9 periods a year OR
  • lengthening of the interval between 2 periods (>35 days)
  • POLYMENORRHEA= shortening of the interval between 2 periods (< 25 days)
  • HYPERMENORRHEA = high menstrual flow (>80 ml)
  • HYPOMENORRHEA= low menstrual flow (<30 ml)
  • METRORRHAGIA= bleeding between normal periods
  • MENORRHAGIA= high menstrual flow (>80 ml) + lengthening of the period’s duration (> 7
  • days)
  • Tanner stages
